tldr: Laforge walks through agentic design patterns (programmatic planning, RAG, progressive disclosure, hierarchical decomposition, LLM-as-judge, goal-oriented planning, agent loops) with Java demos in LangChain4j and ADK for Java.
summary: Guillaume Laforge, a Google Cloud developer advocate and committer on LangChain4j and ADK for Java, frames an agent as an LLM brain plus memory, tools, planning and a loop toward a goal, and lists the concerns that patterns address: planning, context engineering (avoiding context rot), tool overload, evaluation and multi-agent orchestration. Security and observability are explicitly out of scope. He describes each pattern by name, problem, solution and trade-offs, starting with what he calls almost an anti-pattern: giving agents full autonomy when the workflow can be drawn as a flowchart.

His 'programmatic' pattern is a deep-research app that simply chains calls: a Gemini Flash call with Google Search proposes subtopics, the Gemini Interactions API launches Google's hosted Deep Research agent (stateful, background, streamed; one run took 43 minutes), another call writes a one-page summary, and Nano Banana draws a sketchnote. No agent framework is needed. He recaps RAG as early context engineering, then explains Anthropic-style skills: only the SKILL.md front-matter description sits in context, the body loads when relevant, and referenced files or scripts load last. A LangChain4j demo loads a 'deslopify' skill from the classpath to tone down an over-excited draft.

Hierarchical decomposition is shown with an ADK comic-strip app: a sequential flow analyses uploaded photos for location and description, then a parallel flow finds nearby points of interest with Google Maps while generating pop-art panels, sharing results through common state. For LLM-as-judge he generates three summaries with a cheap Flash model, has a small-model judge pick the best, then compares it with a large-model summary. By his prices (about $0.30 per million input tokens for Flash-Lite against $2 for the large model), three small summaries cost less than one big one, and the small model won roughly one time in three.

Goal-oriented action planning, which he credits to Rod Johnson's Embabel and which LangChain4j and ADK for Java adopted, declares each agent's input and output keys and lets an A*-style planner chain agents to reach a goal, such as an infographic or a YouTube Shorts script, from different starting inputs. He ends with a coding-agent loop inspired by Max Rydahl Andersen's minimal Java agent: a supervisor delegating to file, system and web sub-agents inside a plain while loop, in a bit over 300 lines of LangChain4j.
keyPoints: If a task can be drawn as a deterministic flowchart, code it programmatically: easier to debug, at the cost of adaptability.
The Gemini Interactions API is stateful and can invoke hosted agents such as Deep Research in background mode with streamed thoughts.
Skills use three-stage progressive disclosure: front-matter description, then the SKILL.md body, then referenced files and scripts.
In LangChain4j, skills are exposed to the model through a skill tool provider that lets it load skills on demand.
Sequential and parallel sub-agent flows in ADK share a common state map; running independent steps in parallel cuts latency.
LLM-as-judge removes human review bottlenecks but is non-deterministic: the same judge can rate the same output differently.
Goal-oriented action planning (GOAP) lets one pool of agents serve different goals by searching a path through their declared inputs and outputs.
A working coding-agent loop with sub-agents fits in about 300 lines of Java with LangChain4j.
takeaways: Reach for plain programmatic orchestration before an agent framework when the steps are known in advance.
Keep tool and skill lists out of the context window until needed, using progressive disclosure.
Try generating several cheap small-model outputs and picking one with a judge before defaulting to the most expensive model.
Declare agent inputs and outputs explicitly so a goal planner, or a future you, can recombine them.

quotes.text: You don't need a real agent or an agent framework for a lot of use cases that benefit from AI integrated in your projects.
There are things where Java is innovating more than what the Python ecosystem is doing.

watchIf: You build agents in Java and want a catalogue of when to use workflows, sub-agents, judges or goal-based planning, with code for each.
